title: Medicare Supplement Insurance Plan Costs
summary: Explains the costs associated with Original Medicare and AARP Medicare Supplement plans and how to choose a plan letter based on premium versus out-of-pocket tradeoffs.

atoms.title: What to weigh when choosing a Medigap plan
atoms.question: What should I consider when choosing a Medicare Supplement plan?
atoms.text: UnitedHealthcare offers a variety of Medicare Supplement plans with different costs and coverage levels. When you choose a Medicare Supplement plan, consider premiums, your out-of-pocket medical expenses, and what Original Medicare will pay for. Your health needs and budget will help you decide which plan might be best for you.

atoms.title: Monthly premium for Medigap
atoms.question: What is the monthly premium on a Medicare Supplement plan?
atoms.text: A monthly premium is the fee you pay to the plan in exchange for coverage. Each Medicare Supplement plan has a different monthly premium.

atoms.title: Part B deductible is $283 in 2026
atoms.question: What is the Medicare Part B deductible in 2026?
atoms.text: A deductible is the amount you pay out-of-pocket for covered services before Medicare and/or your Medicare Supplement plan begins to pay. Most Medicare Supplement plans provide coverage for your Part A hospital deductible. In most cases you're responsible for your Medicare Part B deductible, which is an annual cost of $283 in 2026.

atoms.title: Copay, coinsurance and out-of-pocket limit
atoms.question: What is the difference between a copay, coinsurance and an out-of-pocket maximum in Medicare?
atoms.text: A copay is a set, flat amount paid each time, such as a $20 copay for each in-office doctor visit. Coinsurance requires you to pay a percentage of the Medicare-approved amount each time. An out-of-pocket limit is a maximum amount of out-of-pocket costs you pay per calendar year. Since Medicare Parts A and B don't have an out-of-pocket maximum, your out-of-pocket medical expenses can add up to hundreds or thousands per year.

atoms.title: Who pays what: Medicare, you and Medigap
atoms.question: How do Medicare Supplement plans provide more coverage than Original Medicare alone?
atoms.text: Medicare pays its share of costs: Part A covers inpatient hospital stays, skilled nursing facility, hospice and home health care, while Part B covers doctor's services, hospital outpatient care, durable medical equipment, home health care and some preventive services. You pay out-of-pocket costs such as deductibles, coinsurance and copayments, plus a monthly premium. Medigap helps fill in some of these gaps, with benefits and costs varying by the plan selected.

atoms.title: Plans G, C and F: most coverage, higher premium
atoms.question: Which Medicare Supplement plans offer the most coverage?
atoms.text: If you prefer more coverage and less out-of-pocket expense, Plans G, C or F may be right for you. These plans typically have a higher premium and offer the most supplemental coverage, paying up to 100% of your out-of-pocket costs for many Medicare-approved services, depending on the plan. Only applicants first eligible for Medicare before 2020 may purchase Plans C and F.

atoms.title: Plans A and B: basic Medigap coverage
atoms.question: What do Medicare Supplement Plans A and B cover?
atoms.text: Medicare Supplement Plan A offers just the Basic Benefits, while Plan B covers Basic Benefits plus a benefit for the Medicare Part A deductible, which could be one of the largest out-of-pocket expenses if you need to spend time in a hospital. Both are options for people who prefer a lower monthly premium with out-of-pocket expenses based on their need.

atoms.title: Plans K, L and N cost-sharing tradeoffs
atoms.question: How do Medicare Supplement Plans K, L and N share costs?
atoms.text: Plans K and L are cost-sharing plans with lower monthly premiums. They pay a percentage of the coinsurance instead of the full amount, and you are responsible for the rest; once the out-of-pocket limit is reached, these plans pay 100% of covered services for the rest of the calendar year. Plan N covers Medicare Part B coinsurance once the Part B deductible is met, but you pay copayments for covered doctor office and emergency room visits in exchange for a mid-level premium.
